diagrams.name: spec-p209-epilepsy-stages
diagrams.title: Epilepsy: stages of a seizure and their signs

labels.answer: Short nose and flat mid face
Normal amount of red blood cell
Anemic amount of red blood cells
Platelets stick to the site and each other
Vasoconstrictors tighten the vessels to slow bleeding
Fibrin strands adhere to the plug to form an insoluble clot

cloze.text: Epilepsy (seizure) is a sudden burst of {{c1::abnormal electrical activity in the brain}}, causing changes in movement, behavior, sensation, or awareness.
Causes of epilepsy include {{c1::brain injury}}, tumors, infections, genetics, and {{c2::high fever}}.
Signs of epilepsy may include sudden stiffening or jerking, loss of consciousness, staring, confusion, or an {{c1::aura}} ({{c2::sensory warning}}).
Epilepsy is managed with {{c1::anti-seizure medications}} (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate) or, in some cases, {{c2::surgery or nerve stimulation devices}}.
Be aware of {{c1::gingival overgrowth}} in epileptic patients taking {{c2::phenytoin}}.
For a patient with epilepsy, use a {{c1::mouth prop}} if needed to prevent injury during treatment.
Schedule {{c1::stress-free}} appointments and avoid {{c2::flashing lights}} for patients with epilepsy.
If a patient seizes in the chair: stop treatment, protect the patient by clearing the area around them, and gently lower the patient to the {{c1::floor}} to prevent falls or injury.
During a seizure, place {{c1::nothing}} in the mouth and never try to {{c2::hold the tongue}}.
During a seizure, gently turn the patient onto their {{c1::side}} to keep the airway clear; if possible, place a pillow or folded towel under the {{c2::head}}.
After a seizure, {{c1::monitor breathing}} and allow the patient to rest; seek emergency help if the patient is injured or {{c2::doesn't recover fully}}.
An {{c1::absence (petit mal)}} seizure is a sudden blank stare that pauses the patient mid-action and is often unnoticed; consciousness is {{c2::briefly lost}}, and it is common in {{c3::children}}.
A {{c1::tonic-clonic (grand mal)}} seizure is {{c2::stiffening (tonic)}} followed by {{c3::shaking (clonic)}}; it may include loss of bladder control.
In a tonic-clonic seizure consciousness is {{c1::completely lost}}; afterwards the patient may be confused — the {{c2::post-ictal}} phase.
An {{c1::atonic}} seizure is a sudden loss of {{c2::muscle tone}}; the patient may collapse without warning, so it often results in {{c3::injury from falls}}. Consciousness is briefly lost.
An {{c1::aura}} is an early warning signal (e.g., smell, taste, sound) just before a seizure begins; consciousness is {{c2::maintained}}. It is not a seizure itself, but may signal one is coming.
Anxiety is a condition where the body stays in a {{c1::heightened state of fear or worry}}, even when there is no immediate danger.
Anxiety can be triggered by stress, trauma, genetics, or a chemical imbalance in the brain — especially low {{c1::GABA}} levels.
Signs of anxiety: {{c1::racing heart}}, {{c2::shortness of breath}}, sweating, nausea, fidgeting, fear, panic, or trouble concentrating.
Anxiety is managed with therapy, stress-reduction techniques, or anti-anxiety medications like {{c1::benzodiazepines}} (e.g., {{c2::lorazepam, diazepam}}).
Anxiety is the {{c1::most common mental health disorder}} in the U.S. and Canada, affecting nearly {{c2::1 in 5}} adults.
{{c1::General anxiety}} is ongoing worry or tension, often without a clear trigger; onset is {{c2::gradual and long-lasting}}, with muscle tension, restlessness and fatigue.
cloze.extra: Example: general worry about health, school and relationships.

cloze.text: A {{c1::panic attack}} is a sudden episode of intense fear and physical symptoms (pounding heart, sweating, shortness of breath, dizziness) that peaks within {{c2::minutes}}.
cloze.extra: Example: a panic attack while sitting in the chair, with no warning.

cloze.text: A {{c1::phobia}} is an extreme fear of a specific object or situation, triggered only by that object or event; it may cause panic, {{c2::avoidance}}, or even fainting.
cloze.extra: Examples: fear of needles, dentists, heights, or blood.

cloze.text: Depression: constant {{c1::low mood}}, sadness and fatigue; low energy and slow thinking; {{c2::withdrawal}}, poor motivation, and appetite or sleep changes.
Depression is treated with {{c1::antidepressants}} (e.g., {{c2::SSRIs}}) and therapy.
Bipolar disorder: mood swings between {{c1::depression}} and {{c2::mania}} (high energy, impulsivity); energy alternates between very low and very high.
{{c1::Bipolar I}}: full episodes of mania and depression.
{{c1::Bipolar II}}: depression with less intense {{c2::hypomania}} (milder elevated mood).
{{c1::Cyclothymia}}: ongoing mood swings with mild highs and lows.
Bipolar disorder is treated with {{c1::mood stabilizers}} (e.g., {{c2::lithium}}), sometimes antipsychotics.
In mood disorders, {{c1::xerostomia}} is a common side effect of medications, and the patient may {{c2::neglect homecare}}.
Alcohol dependence is a long-term brain disorder in which the body needs alcohol to function; it disrupts brain chemicals like {{c1::GABA}} and {{c2::dopamine}}, reinforcing cravings.
For alcohol-dependent patients, avoid {{c1::alcohol-containing products}} such as mouthrinses.
Avoid {{c1::nitrous oxide}} in an alcohol-dependent patient if {{c2::liver damage}} is suspected — the book says it may not be metabolized properly and can increase toxicity.
Alcohol-dependent patients: look for malnutrition, especially vitamin {{c1::B1 (thiamine)}} deficiency, which can affect healing, immunity and oral tissue health.
{{c1::Screen for oral cancer}} in alcohol-dependent patients, especially if alcohol is combined with {{c2::tobacco}}.
An alcohol-dependent patient may neglect hygiene or miss appointments — use a {{c1::nonjudgmental}} tone.
{{c1::Fetal alcohol syndrome}}: alcohol exposure during pregnancy causes brain damage, learning delays, malocclusion, facial signs, {{c2::cleft palate}} and tooth malformations.
Heroin, morphine and fentanyl are {{c1::opioids (narcotics)}}; their pupil sign is {{c2::miosis}}.
Opioid key effects: sedation, pain relief and {{c1::respiratory depression}}; fentanyl is {{c2::50–100x}} stronger than morphine.
cloze.extra: Fentanyl is fully synthetic; a tiny amount can slow or stop breathing.

cloze.text: Opioid oral findings: xerostomia, {{c1::sugar cravings}}, {{c2::bruxism}}, fungal infections and oral neglect.
Opioid dental concerns: poor healing, sedation risk, infection, and {{c1::overdose risk}} with fentanyl.
Cocaine is a {{c1::stimulant}} with mydriasis; key effects are an intense high, {{c2::vasoconstriction}}, energy and a crash.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Cocaine = Camera flash → big pupils.

cloze.text: Cocaine oral findings: xerostomia, {{c1::palatal perforation}}, and high caries.
{{c1::Methamphetamine}} is a stimulant with mydriasis; key effects: long high, {{c2::paranoia}}, aggression, hyperactivity.
Methamphetamine oral findings: xerostomia, "{{c1::meth mouth}}", severe erosion, bruxism; dental concerns: anxiety, soft enamel, {{c2::rampant decay}}.
Ecstasy (MDMA) is a {{c1::stimulant + hallucinogen}} with mydriasis; key effects: mood boost, {{c2::empathy}}, sensory distortion.
Ecstasy (MDMA) oral findings: xerostomia, bruxism, {{c1::TMJ strain}}, jaw pain; dental concerns: dry mouth, clenching, and stress management needed.
Hallucinogens (e.g., {{c1::LSD, mushrooms}}) cause mydriasis, hallucinations, and altered time/body awareness.
Hallucinogen oral findings: xerostomia, {{c1::tongue burns}}, poor hygiene; dental concerns: unpredictable behavior and {{c2::sensory sensitivity}}.
Smoking tobacco reduces salivary flow (xerostomia) due to {{c1::heat and nicotine}}.
Vaping causes xerostomia due to {{c1::propylene glycol}}, a drying agent.
Marijuana xerostomia is worsened by {{c1::THC}}'s effect on salivary glands.
Smoking is a {{c1::major}} periodontal risk factor: {{c2::vasoconstriction}} → poor healing, deep pockets.
Vaping: early data suggest increased {{c1::periodontal disease}} risk due to inflammation and dry mouth. Marijuana is linked to {{c2::gingival inflammation}}, plaque and poor oral hygiene.

Caries risk is elevated especially with {{c1::smokeless tobacco}} (sugar + dry mouth); vaping is a possible risk from {{c2::sweetened e-liquids}} and an altered microbiome; marijuana has mixed results (higher sugar intake, dry mouth).
Tobacco carries a high oral cancer risk — tobacco smoke has carcinogens like {{c1::nitrosamines}}.
Oral cancer risk of vaping is still under research — {{c1::less than tobacco, but not zero}}; THC smoke contains carcinogens, though evidence is less conclusive.
Other oral lesions of smoking: nicotine stomatitis, leukoplakia, {{c1::smoker's melanosis}}, hairy tongue.
Vaping lesions: ulcerations, {{c1::chemical burns}}, nicotine stomatitis-like lesions. Marijuana lesions: {{c2::leukoedema}}, hyperpigmentation, sometimes pre-cancerous lesions.
Halitosis is common with smoking, reported with vaping, and common with marijuana, especially {{c1::habitual use}}.
Tooth discoloration: yes with smoking; possible with vaping from {{c1::e-juice pigments or nicotine}}; marijuana often causes {{c2::yellow-brown}} staining from smoke deposits.
Anemia: the blood lacks enough healthy {{c1::red blood cells}} to carry oxygen to tissues, causing weakness and fatigue.
Anemia can result from blood loss, {{c1::iron deficiency}}, {{c2::vitamin B12 or folate deficiency}}, or chronic disease.
Contributors to anemia: poor diet, {{c1::heavy menstruation}}, ulcers, {{c2::pregnancy}}, malabsorption, or bone marrow disorders.
Signs of anemia: fatigue, {{c1::pale skin or mucosa}}, shortness of breath, dizziness, and {{c2::cold hands/feet}}.
Anemia treatment depends on the type — iron supplements, vitamin therapy, {{c1::blood transfusion}}, or treating the underlying condition.
Anemia dental implications: look for {{c1::pale oral tissues}}, especially the gingiva and tongue; patients may feel fatigued or require {{c2::shorter appointments}}.
In anemia, watch for {{c1::burning mouth syndrome}} or {{c2::atrophic glossitis}} (smooth, red tongue).
Iron-deficiency anemia is acquired (diet, blood loss, pregnancy): not enough iron to make hemoglobin → {{c1::small, pale RBCs}}; symptoms: fatigue, cold hands, {{c2::brittle nails}}.
Oral impact of iron-deficiency anemia: pale mucosa, {{c1::burning mouth}}, {{c2::smooth tongue}}.
Pernicious anemia is acquired — an {{c1::autoimmune}} condition blocks {{c2::B12}} absorption → large, immature RBCs and {{c3::nerve issues}}.
Pernicious anemia symptoms: fatigue, {{c1::numbness}}, memory loss; oral impact: {{c2::red, beefy tongue}}, loss of papillae.
Folate-deficiency anemia is acquired (poor intake, {{c1::alcoholism}}, pregnancy): lack of folate ({{c2::B9}}) → large, immature RBCs.
Folate-deficiency anemia symptoms: fatigue, poor healing, {{c1::irritability}}; oral impact: {{c2::glossitis}}, ulcers, delayed healing.
Sickle cell anemia is {{c1::inherited}} (abnormal gene from both parents): {{c2::hemoglobin S}} causes sickle-shaped RBCs that block vessels.
Sickle cell anemia symptoms: {{c1::pain crises}}, swelling, delayed growth; oral impact: pale gingiva, delayed eruption, "{{c2::step-ladder}}" bone pattern on X-ray.
{{c1::Aplastic}} anemia (acquired or inherited — toxins, immune attack, virus): the {{c2::bone marrow stops producing}} enough blood cells.
Aplastic anemia symptoms: fatigue, infections, bleeding; oral impact: {{c1::petechiae}}, bleeding gums, ulcers.
{{c1::Hemolytic}} anemia (either — genetics, e.g., {{c2::thalassemia}}, or immune diseases): the body destroys RBCs early → less oxygen, more {{c3::bilirubin}}.
Hemolytic anemia symptoms: fatigue, {{c1::jaundice}}, dark urine; oral impact: {{c2::yellow mucosa}}, delayed healing.
Leukemia is a cancer of the {{c1::white blood cells}} in which the bone marrow makes too many abnormal WBCs, crowding out healthy cells and weakening immunity.
The bone marrow makes red blood cells (carry {{c1::oxygen}}), white blood cells (fight {{c2::infection}}), and platelets (help with {{c3::clotting}}).
The exact cause of leukemia is unknown; it may be linked to genetic changes, {{c1::radiation}}, or {{c2::chemical exposure}}.
In leukemia the WBCs are {{c1::immature and non-functional}}, leading to infection risk and poor blood cell balance.
Signs of leukemia: fatigue, frequent infections, {{c1::easy bruising}}, fever, {{c2::swollen lymph nodes}}, and weight loss.
Leukemia treatment — chemotherapy, radiation, bone marrow transplant — all {{c1::suppress immunity}} during treatment.
In leukemia, {{c1::gingival enlargement}} may occur from {{c2::leukemic infiltration}}, not plaque — even with good oral hygiene.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "Leukemia = Leaky Gums" — leuk = white blood cells, but also leaky as in bleeding gums and loose defense in the mouth.

cloze.text: Chemotherapy and radiation can cause {{c1::oral mucositis}} (painful ulceration and inflammation), xerostomia if salivary glands are affected, delayed healing, and increased infection risk.
In leukemia, monitor for oral infections like {{c1::Candida}}, {{c2::herpes simplex}}, and bacterial overgrowth — all worsen with immune suppression.
Delay elective care if the leukemia patient has low WBCs ({{c1::neutropenia}}) or low platelets ({{c2::thrombocytopenia}}) — always consult an {{c3::oncologist}}.
During leukemia treatment, recommend {{c1::soft brushes}}, {{c2::bland rinses}}, and pain-relieving gels to support hygiene.

In the clotting process, the {{c1::clotting cascade}} is a chain reaction of clotting factors — including Factor VIII (Hemophilia A) or Factor IX (Hemophilia B) — that activate in sequence; in hemophilia this step {{c2::fails and the cascade stops early}}.
Hemophilia is a genetic bleeding disorder in which the blood lacks {{c1::clotting factors}}, making it hard to stop bleeding.
Hemophilia is caused by a genetic mutation passed on the {{c1::X chromosome}}.
Hemophilia A = Factor {{c1::VIII}} deficiency; Hemophilia B ({{c2::Christmas disease}}) = Factor {{c3::IX}} deficiency.
cloze.extra: These are the most common types.

cloze.text: In hemophilia, {{c1::platelets}} are normal, but the {{c2::clotting cascade}} is disrupted, so blood forms weak or no clots.
Signs of hemophilia: prolonged bleeding after injury, frequent nosebleeds, {{c1::joint swelling}} from internal bleeding, easy bruising.
Hemophilia: do not probe aggressively or perform procedures without {{c1::medical clearance}}; always consult a {{c2::hematologist}} before extractions or scaling.
{{c1::Spontaneous gingival bleeding}} can occur in hemophilia; reinforce gentle home care.
In hemophilia, avoid {{c1::block anesthesia}} unless the patient is cleared and {{c2::factor}} is administered.
Hemophilia: use local measures to control bleeding — pressure and {{c1::hemostatic agents}}; in some cases antifibrinolytic drugs (e.g., {{c2::tranexamic acid}}) may be prescribed before care.
Queen Victoria of England had hemophilia {{c1::B}} (Christmas disease), known as {{c2::"the royal disease"}}; she passed the gene to royal families through her children.
cloze.extra: Did you know (book): her son Prince Leopold (UK) had hemophilia and died of a brain hemorrhage; daughter Alice passed it to the German royal family, daughter Beatrice to the Spanish royal family; granddaughter Alexandra married the Russian Tsar — their son Tsarevich Alexei had severe hemophilia. (Victoria herself was a carrier.)

cloze.text: {{c1::Von Willebrand disease}} is the most common inherited bleeding disorder.
Von Willebrand factor (vWF) helps {{c1::platelets stick}} and stabilizes {{c2::Factor VIII}}.
Von Willebrand disease is caused by a genetic mutation affecting vWF production or function; it affects both {{c1::males and females}}.
In von Willebrand disease, platelets are normal but vWF is missing or defective, so the {{c1::platelet plug}} is weak and Factor VIII {{c2::breaks down faster}}.
Signs of von Willebrand disease: easy bruising, frequent {{c1::nosebleeds}}, and prolonged bleeding after cuts or dental procedures.
Von Willebrand disease: delay invasive care unless {{c1::cleared by a physician}} and clotting is supported; avoid block anesthesia if bleeding is uncontrolled.
Unusual bleeding during cleanings or extractions may be the {{c1::first sign}} of hemophilia or von Willebrand disease — making dentistry a key point of early detection.
{{c1::Agranulocytosis}} is a severe reduction in granulocytes (especially {{c2::neutrophils}}); the count is often < {{c3::100/µL}}.
{{c1::Cyclic neutropenia}} is an inherited disorder with cyclical drops in neutrophil count; the count drops to < {{c2::500/µL}} for {{c3::2–3 days}}, then returns to normal.

basic.front: Board Alert: why does it matter that a patient takes antidepressants?
basic.back: Antidepressants cause dry mouth (xerostomia) → higher caries risk.
basic.extra: Book's Board Alert: always ask how a condition relates to dentistry — that connection is how you solve case studies.

basic.front: Why do alcohol-dependent patients have more dry mouth and caries?
basic.back: Alcohol is a diuretic and slows saliva production → dry mouth, increased caries and higher risk of oral infections.

basic.front: Why is heroin more dangerous than morphine?
basic.back: Heroin is chemically modified morphine that enters the brain faster → more intense high, but much higher risk of addiction and overdose (why morphine is legal in hospitals and heroin is not).

basic.front: A patient used cocaine in the past 24 hours. What must you avoid in the local anesthetic, and why?
basic.back: Avoid epinephrine — increased blood pressure risk.
A combination of factors: acidic chemicals in the drug erode enamel; severe xerostomia; sugar cravings; neglected oral hygiene; bruxism from increased anxiety → rampant decay.

basic.front: Why is spontaneous bleeding common in leukemia?
basic.back: Low platelet count — abnormal WBCs crowd the bone marrow, leaving less room for platelets (and RBCs and normal immune cells).
basic.extra: Book: this causes bleeding, fatigue and a weakened immune system — in the mouth: spontaneous bleeding, swollen gums, slow healing.

basic.front: Don't be confused: how does the pattern of cyclic neutropenia differ from agranulocytosis?
basic.back: Cyclic neutropenia has a predictable pattern of low neutrophils every few weeks; agranulocytosis is typically sudden or ongoing with no regular cycle.

mcq.question: During scaling, a patient begins a tonic-clonic seizure. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Place a bite block between the teeth to protect the tongue
B. Hold the patient's arms and legs still
C. Stop treatment, clear the area and protect the patient
D. Call 911 at the first sign of the seizure
mcq.answer: C. Stop treatment, clear the area and protect the patient
mcq.explanation: Stop treatment and protect the patient by clearing the area (lowering them to the floor). Never put anything in the mouth or hold the tongue; call 911 only if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes.

mcq.question: A patient with epilepsy has firm, enlarged gingiva. Which anti-seizure medication is MOST likely responsible?
mcq.explanation: Phenytoin is associated with gingival overgrowth. Carbamazepine and valproate are also anti-seizure drugs, but the book links gingival overgrowth to phenytoin.

mcq.question: A patient avoids dental care because of an extreme fear of needles and nearly fainted at her last visit. This BEST describes:
mcq.explanation: A phobia is extreme fear triggered only by a specific object or situation (needles, dentists, blood) and can cause avoidance or fainting; a panic attack comes on suddenly without a specific trigger.

mcq.question: A patient's medication list includes lithium. Which condition is she MOST likely being treated for?
mcq.explanation: Lithium is a mood stabilizer, the treatment for bipolar disorder. Depression is treated with antidepressants such as SSRIs.

mcq.question: Which home-care product should be AVOIDED for a patient recovering from alcohol dependence?
mcq.explanation: Avoid alcohol-containing products like mouthrinses in alcohol-dependent patients; the other products contain no alcohol.

mcq.question: A patient has a palatal perforation and dilated pupils and admits using a drug 6 hours ago. Which is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Use plain anesthetic without epinephrine
B. Use extra epinephrine for hemostasis
C. Proceed normally; the drug has no dental implications
D. Give nitrous oxide to calm the patient
mcq.answer: A. Use plain anesthetic without epinephrine
mcq.explanation: Palatal perforation and mydriasis point to cocaine. Avoid epinephrine if cocaine was used in the past 24 h because of increased BP risk (cocaine already causes vasoconstriction).

mcq.question: A sedated patient with pinpoint pupils, xerostomia and bruxism is MOST likely using:
mcq.explanation: Opioids (heroin, morphine, fentanyl) cause sedation and miosis. Stimulants such as cocaine, meth and MDMA cause mydriasis (dilated pupils).

mcq.question: A patient who vapes daily complains of dry mouth. Which e-cigarette ingredient is MOST responsible?
mcq.explanation: Propylene glycol is a drying agent in e-liquids. Nitrosamines are the carcinogens in tobacco smoke; THC causes dry mouth in marijuana users.

mcq.question: A patient reports numbness and memory loss; her tongue is red and beefy with loss of papillae. Which anemia is MOST likely?
mcq.explanation: Pernicious anemia (autoimmune block of B12 absorption) causes nerve issues (numbness, memory loss) and a red, beefy tongue. Iron-deficiency gives a pale, smooth tongue and no nerve signs.

mcq.question: Radiographs show a "step-ladder" trabecular bone pattern and delayed eruption. Which condition is MOST likely?
mcq.explanation: The step-ladder bone pattern on X-ray, pale gingiva and delayed eruption are the oral impact of sickle cell anemia.

mcq.question: A patient undergoing chemotherapy for leukemia has thrombocytopenia and is scheduled for elective scaling. The hygienist should:
options: A. Proceed with scaling and use extra pressure for hemostasis
B. Delay elective care and consult the oncologist
C. Prescribe an alcohol-containing rinse before scaling
D. Scale only the anterior teeth
mcq.answer: B. Delay elective care and consult the oncologist
mcq.explanation: Delay elective care when platelets (thrombocytopenia) or WBCs (neutropenia) are low, and always consult the oncologist.

mcq.question: A patient with hemophilia A needs quadrant scaling that would require an inferior alveolar nerve block. Which is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Give the block; hemophilia affects only platelets
B. Consult the hematologist; block only after clearance and factor replacement
C. Use an alcohol-containing rinse to reduce bleeding
D. Probe aggressively to assess bleeding first
mcq.answer: B. Consult the hematologist; block only after clearance and factor replacement
mcq.explanation: Avoid block anesthesia unless the patient is cleared and factor is administered; always consult a hematologist before scaling. In hemophilia platelets are normal — the clotting cascade is the problem.

mcq.question: A patient's neutrophil count falls below 500/µL for 2–3 days about every 3 weeks, then returns to normal. This is MOST consistent with:
mcq.explanation: A predictable ~21-day cycle of low neutrophils is cyclic neutropenia; agranulocytosis is sudden or ongoing with no regular cycle and counts often < 100/µL.
